new_statements.quote: According to Allen (1974, 111), Sɛlɛɛ has four distinctive phonetic tones: high (H), mid (M), low (L2) and extra low (L1), and “there is no phonologically significant downstep or downdrift” (see Allen 1974, for an extensive discussion of tonal behavior in context). Lexical words in isolation may contain one, two or three of these tones but the possible sequences are restricted. Tones are used in Sɛlɛɛ for lexical contrast, as illustrated by the sets of minimal pairs in (1), and also for grammatical function, as in (2) and (3) below.
new_statements.citation: Agbetsoamedo, Yvonne. 2014. Aspects of the Grammar and Lexicon of Sɛlɛɛ. Doctoral thesis in Linguistics, Stockholm University (DiVA diva2:742036), comprehensive summary, section 2.1.4 Tones.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Selee is described as a tone language with four level tones (H, M, L, extra-low) carrying lexical and grammatical contrasts; neither this description nor Maddieson & Gordon (1996: 151, 'Sele is a tonal language with lexical contrasts both in nouns and verbs depending on tonal differences') says anything about word stress, accent or prominence, so no stress placement rule can be stated from the accessible sources.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any accessible source.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: Agbetsoamedo notes possible tone sequences on words are restricted and that Selee appears unique among GTM languages in having four non-derived tones; Maddieson & Gordon suspect Heine's contour tones are derived and that Allen's extra-low is in complementary distribution with low.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical words in isolation; nouns and verbs); tone also used for grammatical marking in verbal paradigms (tense/aspect, negation). Agbetsoamedo's four-tone inventory is explicitly taken over from Allen 1974: 111, so that part is second-hand within a first-hand description.
new_statements.identity_note: Both opened sources describe Sɛlɛɛ/Sele of Santrokofi (villages Benua, Bume, Gbodome, north of Hohoe, Volta Region, Ghana) = sele1249 [snw]; no dialect split reported. The name 'Sele' (Maddieson & Gordon) and 'Sɛlɛɛ'/'Selee' (Agbetsoamedo, Glottolog) refer to the same language. The tone inventory quoted from Agbetsoamedo is explicitly credited to Allen 1974: 111.

sources.note: Section 2.1 Phonology (pp. 10-19) covers consonants, vowels, ATR harmony and tones (2.1.4, pp. 14-15): Sɛlɛɛ has four distinctive tones (H, M, L, extra-low, after Allen 1974:111), no downstep/downdrift, tone contrasts lexical and grammatical. The words 'stress', 'accent', 'prominence' do not occur anywhere in the file; no word-stress statement. DiVA itself refuses our machine; copy taken from the Wayback Machine snapshot of 2023-12-08.

sources.citation: Maddieson, Ian & Matthew Gordon. 1996. Notes on the phonetics of Sele, with particular attention to vowels. UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 93 (Fieldwork Studies of Targeted Languages IV): 149-163. (Glottolog lists it as WPP 95, 1997; the volume itself is No. 93, Dec. 1996.)
sources.note: Sec. 2.3 Tones, p. 151: 'Sele is a tonal language with lexical contrasts both in nouns and verbs depending on tonal differences'; five tones after Heine (H, M, L level plus falling/rising contours), Allen's extra-low treated as a variant of low; authors call their own tone transcription impressionistic. No mention of stress, accent or prominence in the paper (scanned of all 15 pages).
